flashcard_questions.q: Where in the periodic table are the transition metals found?
flashcard_questions.a: In the central block, between Group 2 and Group 3.

flashcard_questions.q: How do the melting points of transition metals compare with Group 1 metals?
flashcard_questions.a: Much higher — iron melts at 1538 °C, but sodium melts at just 98 °C.

flashcard_questions.q: How reactive are transition metals compared with Group 1 metals?
flashcard_questions.a: Much less reactive — they do not react vigorously with water or oxygen.

flashcard_questions.q: Which transition metal is the catalyst in the Haber process?
Which transition metal catalyses the hydrogenation of vegetable oils into margarine?
Which transition metal is used in the catalytic converter of a car exhaust?
Why can iron form two different sets of coloured compounds?
flashcard_questions.a: Transition metals form ions with different charges, here Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.

flashcard_questions.q: What charge do the ions of Group 1 metals always carry?
What size range defines a nanoparticle?
What is the diameter range of fine particles?
What happens to the surface area to volume ratio as a particle gets smaller?
Why is a nanoparticle more reactive than the same material in bulk?
flashcard_questions.a: A far greater proportion of its atoms sit on the surface, where they can react.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are titanium dioxide nanoparticles used in sunscreen rather than the bulk powder?
flashcard_questions.a: They are transparent, so they block UV without leaving a white layer on the skin.

flashcard_questions.q: What health risk is linked to breathing in nanoparticles?
flashcard_questions.a: They may damage the lungs in a similar way to asbestos fibres.
